name: Rear Naked Choke from Russian Cowboy
description: Master the Rear Naked Choke from Russian Cowboy. Learn setup mechanics, chin clearing, grip transitions, and finishing details from single-hook back control.
overview:
The Rear Naked Choke from Russian Cowboy exploits the asymmetric single-hook back control to establish a blood choke while the opponent manages competing threats from the leg entanglement. Unlike the standard RNC from full back control with both hooks, this variant uses the Russian Cowboy's diagonal body mechanics to create rotational exposure of the neck. The single leg hook pulls the opponent's hips in one direction while the choking arm drives across from the opposite side, generating a stretching force that opens the neck and prevents the defensive curl.

The setup sequence requires careful grip transition from the riding seatbelt to choking configuration without sacrificing chest-to-back contact. The Russian Cowboy rider must clear the chin line using the free hand while maintaining hook depth with the leg—a coordination challenge that distinguishes this variant from standard back mount applications. The position's inherent instability compared to full back control means the window for choke insertion is narrower, demanding precise timing during the opponent's defensive transitions.

Strategically, the RNC threat serves as the primary fork in the Russian Cowboy attack tree. When the opponent prioritizes neck defense, they expose truck entries, calf slicers, and crucifix transitions. When they prioritize escaping the hook, the neck opens for the choke. This constant threat cycling between upper and lower body attacks makes Russian Cowboy a complete offensive position rather than merely a transitional state.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from blood choke
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate to 30 seconds with proper release

injury_risks.injury: Trachea damage from improper forearm placement
Carotid artery injury from excessive force

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum in training. Never snap or jerk the choke. Partner should have full awareness of pressure building.
tap_signals: Verbal tap (say 'tap' or make any verbal sound)
Physical hand tap on opponent's body or mat
Going limp or loss of consciousness
Any distress signal or unusual sound
release_protocol: Immediately release choking arm upon tap signal
Remove hooks and body triangle if present
Gently guide partner to side-lying recovery position
Monitor consciousness and breathing for 30 seconds
If partner was unconscious, keep them lying down until fully alert
Never allow unconscious partner to stand immediately
training_restrictions: Never use competition speed or intensity in drilling
Never apply the choke to the trachea or windpipe
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with both hands
Stop immediately if partner makes any distress sound
Never hold a choke past the tap for any reason
Beginners must practice with extremely slow progression only

attacker.name: Rear Naked Choke from Russian Cowboy Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the Rear Naked Choke from Russian Cowboy. Setup mechanics, chin clearing, and progressive finishing squeeze from single-hook back control.
attacker.overview: The Rear Naked Choke from Russian Cowboy demands precise grip management during the transition from riding control to choking position. The single-hook configuration creates a unique mechanical advantage where the leg hook generates rotational pressure that exposes the opponent's neck while preventing their primary escape direction. Unlike standard back mount RNC where both hooks provide symmetrical base, the Russian Cowboy attacker must coordinate asymmetric forces—hook tension pulling hips, chest pressure controlling the spine, and the choking arm driving across the carotid arteries. Mastering this coordination transforms Russian Cowboy from a transitional control into a direct finishing platform.
key_principles: Maintain chest-to-back pressure throughout the entire grip transition to prevent the opponent from creating separation or turning
Use the single leg hook to generate diagonal stretch that exposes the neck and prevents the opponent from curling defensively
Transition the choking arm incrementally—secure elbow position first, then deepen hand placement—rather than lunging for the neck
Keep the free leg posted tight against the opponent's body to maintain base and prevent rolls during the finishing sequence
Apply the choke as a blood strangle targeting both carotid arteries simultaneously, positioning the forearm blade against the neck and never the trachea
Use your head as a control point by pressing your temple into the back of the opponent's skull to prevent defensive head turns
setup_requirements: Established Russian Cowboy position with secure chest-to-back contact and the leg hook engaged at thigh depth or deeper
Seatbelt grip with the choking-side arm routed over the opponent's shoulder and the underhook arm beneath the armpit
Opponent's near-side arm controlled or trapped to prevent effective two-on-one grip defense against the choking arm
Head positioned on the choking-arm side to block the opponent's defensive shoulder shrug and chin tuck toward that side
Free leg posted on the mat close to opponent's body to provide stable base throughout the transition to finishing grips

execution_steps.description: With chest firmly connected to the opponent's back, establish a seatbelt grip with your choking arm over their shoulder and underhook arm beneath their armpit. Clasp hands together on their sternum to lock the control configuration before initiating any choke attempt. Confirm your hook is engaged at thigh depth.
execution_steps.timing: Establish before beginning attack - maintain 3-5 seconds to confirm stability

execution_steps.description: Use your overhook hand to cup the opponent's forehead or jaw and rotate their head away from your choking arm side. Simultaneously press your temple firmly into the back of their skull to prevent them from tucking their chin back toward the choking side. This creates the gap needed for forearm insertion across the neck.
execution_steps.timing: 1-2 seconds of head control before threading arm

execution_steps.description: Slide your forearm blade across the exposed side of the opponent's neck, covering one carotid artery with the radius bone. Position the crook of your elbow directly beneath the chin rather than across the trachea, ensuring the bicep muscle closes against the opposite carotid artery when the arm bends.
execution_steps.timing: Smooth insertion over 1-2 seconds, adjusting depth before locking

execution_steps.description: Bring your choking hand to grip your opposite bicep and place your free hand flat behind the opponent's head or on their crown. This figure-four configuration creates the mechanical compression needed to close both carotid arteries simultaneously while the supporting hand drives the head forward into the forearm blade.
execution_steps.timing: Lock grip within 1 second of arm insertion to prevent defensive hand fighting

execution_steps.description: Increase pressure through your leg hook by pulling the opponent's hips toward you while simultaneously driving your chest forward into their upper back. This diagonal stretch extends their body along two opposing axes, preventing the defensive curl that would relieve pressure on the neck and creating structural tension that amplifies the choke.
execution_steps.timing: Begin stretch simultaneously with grip lock

execution_steps.description: Expand your chest against their back while squeezing your elbows together and driving the back of their head forward with your free hand. Build choking pressure progressively over three to five seconds—never jerk or snap the squeeze. The combination of chest expansion, elbow compression, and head drive creates multilateral pressure on both carotid arteries.
execution_steps.timing: 3-5 seconds progressive application, monitoring for tap throughout

execution_steps.description: The moment you feel or hear any tap signal—hand tap, foot tap, verbal tap, or observe your partner going limp—immediately release the choking arm and remove all pressure. Guide your partner to a side-lying recovery position and monitor their consciousness and breathing for at least thirty seconds before allowing them to sit up.
execution_steps.timing: Immediate release with zero delay upon any tap signal

common_counters.counter: Two-on-one grip fighting on the choking arm wrist before figure-four is locked
common_counters.your_response: Strip their grip by rotating your wrist and re-inserting from a different angle, or switch to a short choke variation by cupping your own wrist instead of grabbing the bicep

common_counters.counter: Chin tuck defense with shoulder shrug to deny the forearm entry across the neck
common_counters.your_response: Use your free hand to cup their forehead and physically rotate their head away, or apply a palm-to-palm squeeze that works over the chin by compressing through the jawline

common_counters.counter: Opponent rolls their body toward the hook side attempting to turn and face you
common_counters.your_response: Follow the roll maintaining chest contact and hook tension—the roll actually feeds into a tighter choke position as you end on top, or transition to truck if they overcommit to the roll

common_counters.counter: Opponent strips the leg hook and shrimps away to create distance for guard recovery
common_counters.your_response: Immediately re-engage the hook by driving your knee back under their thigh while pulling with your seatbelt to collapse the space they created, or follow into standard back control with both hooks

common_errors.error: Reaching for the neck before clearing the chin line with proper head control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent tucks chin and establishes two-on-one wrist defense, stalling the attack and allowing escape preparation
common_errors.correction: Always use your free hand to cup the forehead and rotate the head away before threading the choking arm across the neck

common_errors.error: Placing the forearm across the trachea instead of positioning the blade against the carotid arteries
common_errors.consequence: Produces painful windpipe compression without effective blood flow restriction, causes potential trachea injury, and gives opponent time to escape
common_errors.correction: Position the blade of the forearm against the side of the neck with the elbow crook centered under the chin, ensuring bicep and forearm close on opposite carotid arteries

common_errors.error: Releasing chest-to-back pressure to reach further around the opponent's neck
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for the opponent to turn their shoulders, establish defensive frames, or escape to guard
common_errors.correction: Maintain chest contact throughout the entire sequence—if you cannot reach the neck, adjust your body angle or deepen your position rather than lifting away

common_errors.error: Squeezing with arms only without engaging the hook stretch or chest expansion
common_errors.consequence: Burns grip endurance rapidly and produces a weaker choke that experienced opponents can weather while preparing their escape
common_errors.correction: Coordinate the finish as a system: expand chest into their back, engage hook to stretch their hips, and squeeze elbows together simultaneously for maximum multilateral compression

common_errors.error: Applying the choke with a sudden jerk or snap instead of progressive pressure
common_errors.consequence: Risk of serious neck injury to training partner and violation of training safety protocols
common_errors.correction: Build pressure progressively over three to five seconds in training, allowing your partner full opportunity to recognize and signal a tap before pressure becomes dangerous

common_errors.error: Neglecting the leg hook during the finishing sequence and allowing it to become shallow
common_errors.consequence: Opponent extracts the hooked leg, eliminates the diagonal stretch advantage, and escapes to guard or turtle
common_errors.correction: Actively maintain hook depth by pulling your heel toward your buttock throughout the choke, using the hook tension to complement the upper body squeeze

training_progressions.focus: Choking arm placement and figure-four lock
training_progressions.description: Practice figure-four grip mechanics and forearm positioning on a compliant partner lying prone. Focus on consistent carotid alignment, progressive squeeze calibration, and proper elbow crook placement beneath the chin. No positional resistance—isolate the finishing mechanic.

training_progressions.focus: Head control sequences from seatbelt to choke
training_progressions.description: Partner defends with chin tuck and shoulder shrug only while you practice the full clearing sequence from Russian Cowboy: forehead cup, head rotation, arm threading, and figure-four lock. Build the muscle memory for smooth transitions between control grips.

training_progressions.focus: Maintaining Russian Cowboy control during choke attempt
training_progressions.description: Partner provides moderate escape resistance including grip fighting and positional movement. Work the complete sequence from seatbelt through finish while maintaining hook depth and chest contact. Develop the coordination of asymmetric upper and lower body forces.

training_progressions.focus: Competition timing, threat cycling, and combination attacks
training_progressions.description: Full resistance positional sparring starting from established Russian Cowboy. Cycle between RNC attempts, truck transitions, and other attacks based on defensive responses. Develop the ability to read defenses and select the highest-percentage attack in real time.

knowledge_assessment.question: What anatomical structures does the Rear Naked Choke from Russian Cowboy specifically target?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The RNC targets both carotid arteries simultaneously using bilateral compression. The forearm blade covers one carotid artery on the side of the neck while the bicep closes against the opposite carotid when the figure-four is squeezed. This bilateral blood flow restriction to the brain causes unconsciousness within seconds. The choke must never target the trachea or windpipe.

knowledge_assessment.question: What control points must be established before attempting the choking sequence from Russian Cowboy?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Five control points must be confirmed: chest-to-back contact preventing separation, seatbelt grip with choking arm over the shoulder and underhook beneath the armpit, the leg hook engaged at thigh depth or deeper, the opponent's near-side arm controlled to prevent two-on-one defense, and head positioned on the choking-arm side to block defensive shoulder shrugs. Attempting the choke without all five increases escape probability significantly.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent's grip fighting suddenly weakens and their arms drop from defending their neck—what should you do immediately?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately check for signs of unconsciousness rather than continuing to squeeze. A sudden drop in defensive effort often indicates the blood choke is taking effect and the opponent may be losing consciousness without being able to tap. Release pressure, check responsiveness by calling their name, and if they are unconscious, place them in recovery position and monitor breathing. Never assume they are giving up—always verify consciousness.

knowledge_assessment.question: At what point in the RNC sequence from Russian Cowboy is the defender effectively past the point of escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Once the figure-four is fully locked with the choking hand gripping the opposite bicep and the free hand positioned behind the head, the defender's escape options drop dramatically. At this stage, two-on-one grip strips become mechanically inefficient against the locked figure-four, and the diagonal stretch from the hook prevents the body curl needed to relieve pressure. The defender's best remaining option is an immediate tap rather than prolonged resistance that risks unconsciousness.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the most dangerous placement error when applying the choking arm and how do you correct it?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Placing the forearm across the trachea instead of against the side of the neck is the most dangerous error. Trachea compression causes extreme pain, potential cartilage damage, and does not effectively restrict blood flow to the brain—meaning the opponent suffers injury without the choke actually working. Correct by positioning the blade of the forearm flat against the lateral neck with the elbow crook centered directly under the chin, so the squeeze closes bicep and forearm against both carotid arteries.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent manages to wedge two fingers under your choking forearm during the squeeze—what grip adjustment prevents them from creating space?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Rather than fighting their fingers directly, shift to a palm-to-palm grip variation by releasing the bicep grip and clasping both hands together behind the opponent's head in a Gable grip or S-grip. This changes the compression vector and eliminates the gap their fingers were exploiting. Simultaneously increase the diagonal stretch through your hook to extend their body, which pulls the neck deeper into whatever grip configuration you hold. Switching grip style is faster than stripping fingers.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the single leg hook specifically contribute to the finishing mechanics of the RNC from Russian Cowboy?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The hook creates a diagonal stretch by pulling the opponent's hips in one direction while the upper body drives the opposite way. This extending force prevents the defensive curl where the opponent tucks their chin and rounds their shoulders to protect the neck. The stretched body position also makes it mechanically harder for the opponent to generate the hip movement needed to escape or the arm strength needed for grip fighting. Without active hook engagement during the squeeze, the choke loses roughly thirty percent of its mechanical efficiency.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why must the RNC be applied progressively over three to five seconds in training rather than snapped on quickly?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Progressive application gives the training partner time to recognize increasing pressure and signal a tap before the choke reaches dangerous levels. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness in as little as four seconds once both carotid arteries are fully compressed. A sudden snap application can render a partner unconscious before they have any opportunity to tap, creating risk of prolonged blood flow restriction, potential brain injury, and secondary injuries from falling. Competition speed application is reserved only for actual competition.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent is defending the RNC by tucking their chin aggressively and pinning it to their chest—what finishing strategy works against this defense?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Apply a palm-to-palm squeeze that compresses through the jawline rather than requiring clean forearm-to-neck contact. Cup your choking hand over the chin area and clasp your other hand over it, then squeeze elbows together while expanding your chest. The pressure transmits through the jaw into the carotid arteries beneath. Alternatively, maintain patient chin-line pressure with your forearm while using the hook stretch to extend their body—the extension gradually weakens their chin tuck as their muscles fatigue under the stretch.

knowledge_assessment.question: What immediate actions must you take if your training partner loses consciousness during RNC application?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately release all choking pressure and remove your arms from around their neck. Gently lower them to the mat and place them in a side-lying recovery position to protect the airway. Call their name and gently shake their shoulder to check responsiveness. Most people regain consciousness within ten to thirty seconds. Do not allow them to stand up immediately after regaining consciousness. If they do not regain consciousness within thirty seconds, call for medical assistance immediately. Stay calm and monitor their breathing continuously.

defender.name: Rear Naked Choke from Russian Cowboy Defender
defender.description: Defend the Rear Naked Choke from Russian Cowboy. Recognition cues, grip fighting, escape paths, and recovery strategies from single-hook back control attacks.
defender.overview: Defending the Rear Naked Choke from Russian Cowboy requires addressing the immediate choking threat while managing the single-hook leg entanglement that defines this position. The asymmetric structure creates both unique dangers and specific escape opportunities not available against conventional dual-hook back control. The primary defensive challenge is that the opponent uses the hook to create a diagonal stretch that opens your neck, making standard chin-tuck defense less effective than against a conventional RNC. Successful defense demands disciplined two-on-one hand fighting to prevent the choking arm from crossing the chin line, combined with calculated hip movement toward the opponent's free leg side to create viable escape angles without feeding into truck transitions.
key_principles: Protect the neck as absolute first priority—hand fighting must begin before the choking arm crosses the chin line, not after
Control the choking-side wrist with a two-on-one grip to mechanically prevent forearm insertion across the neck
Tuck chin to the choking-arm side and pin it tightly to your shoulder to deny the opening the attacker needs
Address the leg hook systematically to eliminate the diagonal stretch that amplifies the choke's effectiveness
Create escape angles by turning toward the opponent's free leg side rather than rolling away from the hook
Maintain controlled breathing to avoid panic-driven energy depletion during sustained defensive sequences
recognition_cues: Opponent's overhook hand releases the seatbelt clasp and begins moving toward your forehead, jaw, or the top of your head
Increased chest pressure against your back combined with the choking-side arm beginning to slide higher over your shoulder
Opponent's head presses harder against the back of your skull, positioning for the head drive that accompanies arm insertion
Subtle increase in leg hook tension as the opponent prepares the diagonal hip stretch that opens space at the neck

defensive_options.action: Two-on-one grip strip on the choking arm wrist before the figure-four locks
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the choking arm begin to slide across your chin line—this is the highest-percentage window for defense
defensive_options.if_successful: Returns to neutral Russian Cowboy position with the choke attempt fully neutralized and attacker must rebuild their setup
defensive_options.risk: If the grip strip fails or is too slow, the attacker may already have sufficient arm depth to lock the figure-four

defensive_options.action: Chin tuck with shoulder shrug to physically block the forearm from crossing the neck
defensive_options.when_to_use: Immediately when you recognize the attacker clearing your chin line—use as first line of defense before committing to grip fighting
defensive_options.if_successful: Denies the opening needed for the choking arm insertion, forcing the attacker to spend time clearing your chin again
defensive_options.risk: Static defense that does not improve your position—the attacker will attempt chin clearing techniques repeatedly

defensive_options.action: Hip escape toward the free leg side when attacker commits both arms to the choking sequence
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker loosens their positional control to commit fully to the choke—the moment their seatbelt breaks or hook lightens
defensive_options.if_successful: Escape to guard position facing the opponent, neutralizing both the back control and the choke threat entirely
defensive_options.risk: If timed poorly before the attacker has truly committed to the choke, they maintain back control with a partially set choking grip

escape_paths: Two-on-one grip fighting to strip the choking arm followed by hip escape toward the free leg side to recover half guard or closed guard
Explosive bridge toward the hook side to create momentary space, then immediately turn into the opponent and establish defensive frames for guard recovery
Systematic hand fighting combined with progressive leg hook extraction to dismantle control points and return to turtle or standing position

favorable_outcomes.how: Strip the choking arm grip with two-on-one defense, create separation through hip escape toward the opponent's free leg side, then turn to face the opponent and close your guard around their waist before they can re-establish back control

common_errors.error: Defending with one hand on the choking wrist instead of committing both hands to the two-on-one grip
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient grip strength against the attacker's figure-four lock—the arm gets pulled across the neck despite the single-hand resistance
common_errors.correction: Always use both hands on the choking wrist for maximum mechanical advantage, gripping with thumbs on the same side for a unified pulling direction

common_errors.error: Rolling away from the hook in panic to escape the choking setup
common_errors.consequence: Feeds directly into the truck position, often tightening the choke by giving the attacker a better finishing angle as they follow the roll
common_errors.correction: Turn toward the opponent's free leg side while maintaining strong defensive frames—this direction does not assist truck entry and may allow guard recovery

common_errors.error: Ignoring the choke setup to focus exclusively on escaping the positional control
common_errors.consequence: Attacker secures the figure-four during the escape attempt and finishes the choke while you are mid-movement and unable to defend
common_errors.correction: Address the choking arm first with two-on-one grip fighting, then work positional escape only after the immediate strangling threat is neutralized

common_errors.error: Extending arms away from the body to push frames against the attacker
common_errors.consequence: Exposes the extended arms to kimura, armbar, or wrist lock counter-attacks while creating no meaningful separation
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows tight to the body and create frames using forearm structure rather than reaching—tight elbows protect against arm attacks while still generating useful leverage

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the earliest physical cues that indicate an RNC is being set up from Russian Cowboy?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The earliest cue is the attacker's overhook hand releasing from the seatbelt clasp and beginning to move toward your forehead or jaw—this indicates they are transitioning from positional control to chin clearing for the choke. Secondary cues include increased chest pressure into your back, the attacker's head pressing harder against your skull to position for the head drive, and increased tension through the leg hook as they prepare the diagonal stretch. Recognizing the seatbelt break is the critical early warning.

knowledge_assessment.question: When should you tap to an RNC from Russian Cowboy and what tap signals are available to you?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Tap immediately when you feel blood flow restriction to your brain—symptoms include tunnel vision, lightheadedness, or a rushing sensation in your ears. Do not wait to see if you can escape once these symptoms appear. Available tap signals include hand tapping the attacker's body or the mat, foot tapping the mat, saying tap verbally, or making any vocal sound. In training, tap early and tap often. An ego-driven late tap risks unconsciousness and the secondary injuries that come with it.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the most effective defensive technique against the RNC from Russian Cowboy and why?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The two-on-one grip on the choking wrist is the highest-percentage defense because it uses both of your arms against one of the attacker's arms, creating a significant mechanical advantage. Grip both hands on the choking wrist with thumbs aligned and pull it below your chin line toward your sternum. This is more effective than chin tucking alone because it actively prevents arm insertion rather than passively blocking it. The defense must be initiated before the figure-four locks—once the figure-four is set, two-on-one becomes insufficient against the locked grip structure.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent has secured the figure-four but has not fully applied the squeeze yet—what is your best defensive option?
knowledge_assessment.answer: With the figure-four already locked, grip stripping becomes very difficult. Your best option is to immediately tuck your chin hard into the crook of their elbow while pulling their choking wrist down with both hands to create any space between their forearm and your neck. Simultaneously begin an explosive hip escape toward their free leg side—this is your last positional escape window before the squeeze tightens. If you cannot create space or escape within a few seconds, tap immediately rather than fighting a locked figure-four to exhaustion and risking unconsciousness.

knowledge_assessment.question: You have been defending the RNC grip fight for thirty seconds and your arms are fatiguing—how should you manage this situation?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Sustained grip fighting against an RNC is an energy battle you will eventually lose if you remain purely defensive. Rather than continuing to grip fight indefinitely, use a brief burst of energy for a decisive escape attempt: bridge hard toward the free leg side while stripping the choking arm and immediately turn to face the opponent. If this escape fails and you are too fatigued to maintain effective two-on-one defense, tap before your grip strength drops below the threshold needed to prevent the choke from locking. Controlled tapping when defense is failing is always preferable to involuntary unconsciousness.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying choke setup cues and maintaining neck protection
training_progressions.description: Partner establishes Russian Cowboy and slowly works through the RNC setup sequence while you practice recognizing each stage: seatbelt break, chin clearing attempt, arm threading. Focus solely on chin tuck, hand positioning, and breathing without attempting escape.

training_progressions.focus: Two-on-one defense and grip strip timing
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts the RNC at moderate speed while you drill the two-on-one wrist grip at each stage of the choke setup. Practice stripping the arm before figure-four locks, during chin clearing, and as a last resort against a partially locked grip. Build muscle memory for immediate grip engagement on recognition.

training_progressions.focus: Combining grip defense with hip escape and guard recovery
training_progressions.description: Partner provides progressive resistance during the full RNC attack sequence. Practice the complete defensive flow: recognize cues, establish two-on-one, strip the grip, then immediately hip escape toward the free leg side to recover guard. Emphasis on seamless transition from hand defense to positional escape without pausing between phases.

training_progressions.focus: Full resistance defense with realistic attack combinations
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring starting from Russian Cowboy with the attacker cycling between RNC, truck entries, and other attacks. Defend all threats while seeking escape opportunities. Develop the ability to read whether the attacker is committing to the choke or transitioning, and choose defensive responses accordingly.
